english: I think an attentive reader may wonder why, although I have divided my little work into a definite number of books, as writers customarily do, I nevertheless settle in one book questions belonging to another. For example, in the third volume I argued that the statement that the Jewish people descended from the one man Abraham (Hebrews 11:12) did not in the slightest shake the apostle’s meaning when he said that sin entered the world through one man (Romans 5:12), a numerical expression that demolished the opinion of original evil. The reader whom I now intend to satisfy may think this should have been placed in the second volume. Let him understand, then, that this faithfulness in replying, by which even things thought to have been passed over are supplied in the following book, causes no disadvantage to the contest. It comes not from confusion caused by haste, but both from the requirements of the subject and from a considered plan. Many great minds offer examples that could justify such a sequence of writing. But it is foolish boasting to call on the resounding names of ancient writers to defend a simple matter, and to make an innocent action look suspicious by defending it.

I therefore ended the second book, which I had devoted to defending the apostle’s statements, when the necessary discussion was complete, so that adding trivial questions would not stretch it to excessive length. But after fulfilling the duty of serious argument, I chose to answer even foolish questions and to take account of the very slowest readers, who can be disturbed even by feeble objections. Accordingly, in the third book I showed how many people could be said to have been born from one. It is also entirely fitting for a following volume to discharge the debt of its predecessor: the books then show a strong agreement with one another, and readers are encouraged to learn the whole work. Even if they consider that some points were postponed in the earlier books, they understand that they were not omitted. Having shown, then, that what we have done accords with the work’s faithfulness and care, let us fight the Manichaeans on behalf of God’s works and laws. From his works we repel the ugliness of natural evil; from his laws, the injustice of deadly judgments. We teach that in the commands of those laws justice has lost none of its goodness, and into the seeds of those works the devil has mixed none of his evil. In short, the laws are worthy of God as ruler, and the works supremely worthy of God as creator.

If you believe these two things, that God’s works are not evil and his judgments are not unjust, the whole doctrine of inherited sin is crushed. Conversely, if the impiety of inherited sin is accepted, these two things, God’s creation and his judgment, through which alone God can be understood, are destroyed.

Let us now weigh the things this slanderer of nature has put together. But to help our reader both understand and distinguish matters entangled in our replies to one another, I will explain the way he fights. He professes to answer writings of mine that he says were sent to him on a short sheet, and he quotes and attacks little pieces of statements attributed to me that are not found in my work.

He therefore says to Valerius: “Notice the arguments by which he thinks he agrees, against us, with the heading set out above. He says, ‘God, who had fashioned Adam from mud, built Eve from a rib and said: She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living’ (Genesis 3:20). That is not actually how it is written, but what does that matter to us? Memory commonly goes wrong over words, provided the meaning is retained. Nor was it God who named Eve Life, but her husband. The text says: ‘And Adam called his wife’s name Life, because she is the mother of all the living’” (Genesis 1:31) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).

What astonishing learning in this teacher, who allows not even the slightest departure from Scripture’s language! He rebukes my ignorance, yet deigns to pardon the lapse of memory through which I had supposedly said that God called the woman by the name Life. He thus used a small opportunity to try to appear both learned and kind. But just as identifying who named the woman is no remarkable feat of diligence, so his shamelessness is intolerable when he wants to forgive something he cannot blame. For my work does not read as his inventions have it. I first quoted the Law’s testimony, where the Creator of all things is shown saying, “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Genesis 2:18). Then I said: “What does this mean, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? Had God made anything that could rightly be called not good, especially when he had made everything not merely good but very good (compare Genesis 1:31)? How, then, does he say, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone’? These words do not criticize the creature’s condition; they show that being alone could have been ruinous for the human race unless a succession of descendants had sprung up through the service of the other sex. For even if Adam may be thought capable of becoming immortal had he not sinned, it is nevertheless clear that he could never have become a father unless he had found a wife. Taken from his side while he slept, she heard at her first naming the work for which she had been prepared: ‘She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living.’ This statement showed that thereafter no human being could either exist or live without coming into existence through the benefit of conception” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12).

It is therefore clear that, although the matter is not very weighty, I said nothing that anyone could criticize without extraordinary shamelessness. The stamp of public falsehood has been branded on this most destitute of men. By trying to give away what he does not possess, he offends in two ways at once: he lacks the right to do it, and he courts applause for his generosity.

added_allusions.reason: God made everything very good.

english: After criticizing this with such solemnity, he proceeds to the rest and tells his patron to attend to what follows. “God, then,” he says, “the creator of male and female, formed organs suited to reproduction.” But after inserting only this much from the beginning of my statement, he omits a very large number of lines. These chiefly stress that souls are newly created and owe nothing either to flesh or to seed. He then adds my words: “Thus he ordained that bodies should be generated from bodies. Yet his active power intervenes in their production, governing everything that exists by the same power with which he created it. If, then, offspring come only through sex, sex only through a body, and a body only through God, who could doubt that fertility is rightly attributed to God?” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12). After quoting this from my work, he commends it, saying that he too acknowledges these statements to be catholic. Who would not then think that the man had changed? But he does not forget himself. He supposes that a perverse doctrine and his sense of shame are in a similar condition: that the doctrine can recover even from its evident destruction, just as his shamelessness grows harder through constant wear. So he approves my statement and, by voluntarily embracing it, drives the blade of an adverse judgment into his own belief. Yet afterward, as though his strength were unimpaired, he imagines that he still has something with which to fight.

He continues as follows: “After these things, which have been said truthfully and catholically—or rather, which are truthfully written in the divine books, but have not been said catholically by this man, because they were not said with the intention of a catholic heart—the Pelagian and Caelestian heresy now begins to be introduced, which is why he said them. For notice what follows.” Here he adds my words again: “What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes, by which he can rightly possess their offspring? Their difference? But that exists in the bodies God made. Their union? But it is defended by the privilege of God’s blessing no less than by his institution. For it is God’s voice that says, ‘A man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24). It is God’s voice that says, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). Or perhaps fertility itself? But that is the very reason marriage was instituted” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.13).

To this he replied that the devil recognizes neither the difference of the sexes, nor their union, nor their fertility as something of his own by which he can rightly possess their offspring. But after acquitting all these things he found something to assign to the devil. He attacked my decency as fear, saying that amid so many functions of bodies and sexes I had been afraid to name the desire of the flesh. This, then, is what he tells his patron against me: “But amid all these things he was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16). The devil is called the ruler of this world. He did not find this desire in the Lord, because the Lord came among human beings as a man without it. Hence the Lord himself says, ‘See, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me’ (John 14:30): nothing, that is, of sin, either inherited at birth or added in the course of life. Among all the natural goods he mentioned, this man was unwilling to name the desire that makes even marriage ashamed, although marriage glories in all those goods. For why is that act of married people withdrawn and hidden even from their children’s eyes, except that their praiseworthy union cannot take place without shameful lust? It was this that made the first people blush when they covered their private parts (Genesis 3:7). Those parts had not previously been shameful, but deserved praise and glory as God’s works” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.13).

Most blessed father Florus, in the four books of my first work I pleaded the case for marriage, for sexual union, for bodies, for the sexes, for God’s work, and finally for God’s reputation. Just as his reputation is necessarily praised by the goodness of his works, so it is wounded when they are defamed. Throughout that entire work, truth that cannot be obscured proved that the devil had added nothing either to the body’s formation or to its sensation. Thus it was thoroughly demonstrated that the belief in inherited sin had been drawn from Manichaeus’s mud.

Although this was established there with the fullest possible treatment, it must also be repeated, briefly, in the present discussion. Let us turn, then, to the man himself, whose learning we are contesting. You agree, surely, that I reasoned correctly: if offspring exist only through sex, sex only through a body, and a body only through God, there can be no doubt that fertility belongs among God’s works. The ruler of darkness recognizes nothing of his own in the sexes by which he could keep their offspring as his rightful property. For their difference belonged to sex, their union to the difference of their organs, and the fruit of fertility to God, who had also established those who generate offspring. Accordingly, nothing remained for which the fertility of sexual union should be awarded to the devil.

What comfort or defense, then, do you think the decency of my language gives you because I did not wish to name the desire of the flesh in this passage? Even if I had passed it over in silence throughout the whole work, that would have brought no blame or injury upon the thing itself. It was being defended under more decent names, and indeed in language perfectly clear to the understanding. Suppose, then, that with more reserve than the subject required I had chosen to veil in silence the name of what we cover with clothing. Must all reason and all truth therefore be thrown away? Must understanding, the judge of matters, therefore lie helpless because there is something that cannot always be brought decently before the ears, just as it cannot always be brought before the eyes? Yet what is ugly about naming the desire of the flesh? I have named it when the occasion required, and you mention it frequently, although you insist that you find it untamable.

A little later comes this: “Through what, then, are infants under the devil? They are born from bodies God made, from the union of sexes that God distinguished in forming them, joined in blessing them, and multiplied by implanting fertility; and God made the infants themselves from the material of seed. If you acknowledge that the material of bodies, their reproductive organs, the union of those organs, the power of seeds, and the form and life of everyone born all exist through God, what do you think is left for which you can transfer so many of God’s works to the devil?” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15). So you call someone else’s argument a heresy as a whole, although you acknowledge that every one of its parts is correct and catholic.

For my conclusion is fortified by such truth that its whole force falls upon you. Unable even to violate it with abuse, you praised it under God’s compulsion; yet you accuse the result to which it leads.

“If, then,” I say, “offspring come only through sex, sex only through a body, and a body only through God, who could doubt that fertility is rightly attributed to God?” This is so certain that it forced even your mouth to praise it. But after paying this passage your tribute, you warn that a heresy is being introduced, although the words I added merely repeated what had come before, with an explanation attached.

For I say: “What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes, so that, as you say, he rightly possesses their offspring? Their difference? But that exists in the bodies God made. Their union? But it is defended by the privilege of God’s blessing no less than by his institution. Or perhaps fertility itself? But that is the very reason marriage was instituted.” What was new here? What disagreed with the previous conclusion you had approved, so that you thought you should blame it after praising it? Certainly nothing. What follows, then, from such disgusting inconsistency? Clearly, since my argument has not changed while your assessment of my words has altered, your intention is utterly foul and your reasoning weak.
And your praise of catholic statements comes from your fear, not your faith.
Your blame of what you have praised therefore comes from frenzy, not judgment.

You will never be free of that frenzy unless you first reject your obscene doctrine. For you are caught between two crushing rocks: the shame of repentance, which Christians nevertheless never reject, and your lack of an argument. You must either follow or tear apart the sound statements that overwhelm you.
translator_notes: The “two crushing rocks” translate an allusion to the Symplegades, the clashing rocks in the story of the Argonauts.

english: Still, let us see which of my statements you have seized on to attack under the name of error. “But amid all these things,” (John 14:30) you say, “he was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world. The devil is called the ruler of this world. He did not find this desire in the Lord, because the Lord came among human beings as a man without it” (1 John 2:16) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.14; compare 1 John 2:16; John 14:30). You certainly said I was introducing a heresy, but you add none of my words to prove it (1 John 2:16; John 14:30).

added_allusions.reason: Desire of the flesh is from the world, not the Father.
The ruler of the world finds nothing in Christ.

english: Instead you say I was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh. If I was unwilling to name it, I kept silent; and if I kept silent, I said nothing for you to criticize. Who, then, persuades someone to adopt an error by keeping silent? What new and previously unheard-of monstrosities of accusation! He says a perverse doctrine is being constructed out of my silence!
Let every sensible person weigh this and laugh at hostility to a speech being displayed under the name of silence. You therefore admit that I said nothing you can refute.

Indeed, by harassing my silence, you have brought out something that could never be defended before, and that now cannot even be concealed, since Manichaeus’s letter, passages from which I quoted in the third book, has become public.

“He was unwilling,” (John 14:30) he says, “to name the desire of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world. The devil is called the ruler of this world. He did not find this desire in the Lord, because the Lord came among human beings as a man without it” (1 John 2:16) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.14; compare 1 John 2:16; John 14:30). In the very words of Manichaeus, then, you profess that the desire of the flesh was made not by God but by the world, whose ruler you nevertheless say is the devil (1 John 2:16; John 14:30).

added_allusions.reason: Desire of flesh is from the world, not the Father.
The ruler of the world finds nothing in Christ.

english: I said that you used language entirely belonging to Manichaeus because, although some of these words occur in the apostle John’s letter, it is certain that this teacher of the Church meant nothing there about the flesh, its sensation, or marital desire like what Manichaeus constructs by appropriating his words. I therefore rightly called them the words of the man whose meaning they served: language should be judged according to the intention behind it. In Saint John these words deserve reverence for their apostolic dignity, because they convey truth; in Manichaeus they appear as obscured traces of those words, not their faithful expression.

For the apostle John was urging the faithful toward the summit of every virtue and stretching their pursuit of holiness to the height of the Lord’s manner of life. To be brief, he embraced under the name of the whole world every attraction of present goods and pleasures: “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him, because everything in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. The world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:15–17). If we look only at the surface of the words, he commands hatred of all the elements and declares that the world and everything in it are not from the Father and should not be loved.

He is certainly an apostle, loved by the Lord Jesus with a special affection (compare John 13:23). Yet if neither the Gospel he wrote nor the weight of his letters revealed his intention, these words I have quoted could count in no way against created things: they would have to give way to all the Scriptures that declare the world was made by God. But he himself secured his position in the revered opening of the Gospel he wrote. “The Word,” he says, “was God. Everything was made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1, 3) (John 13:23). And afterward: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in this world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:9–10). Again: “The Word became flesh, to dwell among us” (John 1:14). These testimonies leave no obscurity in his meaning. They show that he knows and proclaims God as creator of the whole world and of everything in it, and thoroughly demonstrate that the Manichaeans have no way into his teaching. For someone who proclaims God as creator of all natures can use the names of substances figuratively to signify excessive desire, without damage to the faith.

added_allusions.reason: John is described as specially loved by Jesus.

english: He therefore commands us not to love the world or the things in it, and says that God’s love cannot be present in lovers of this age. But in saying that love must be withdrawn from the world, he does not mean us to understand that its creator is someone other than the true God. Rather, he wants the faithful to recognize that no desires of the present life should be preferred to virtues. Their minds must not become so occupied with acquiring wealth or pursuing pleasures that they are drawn away from the vigor of Christian philosophy, which is the true philosophy. “For everything in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. The world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:16–17). By the name “world,” then, he indicated the conduct of people who suppose there is nothing after this life, and the various displays and luxuries of mortals.

For he had also said in his Gospel: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10) (Matthew 10:37). He certainly did not mean that the elements, which lack reason, could appear capable of knowing or denying Christ. He meant the multitude of unbelievers to be designated by the name “world.” In the same way here, too, he says that everything in the world—that is, every sort of person so devoted to pleasures that they measure all the goods of a rational creature by the trappings of power, loads of wealth, or the senses—has swollen with hateful pride. This is not from God, meaning it does not please God, but is from the world: it is conceived through the perversity of the human will. “Therefore,” he says in effect, “it must not corrupt you by making you imitate it. Whoever does God’s will comes to share eternal blessedness and does not fly past with the frailty of present things.”

So the apostle John commanded the world to be hated in the same way that the Lord in the Gospel showed that not only our body but even our soul itself must be hated: “Whoever does not hate father or brother, and even his own soul as well, is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:26; compare Matthew 10:37). Yet the mind of a believer certainly cannot hate itself when, out of the most thoughtful love, it purchases its own happiness even through pains and dangers. What, then, have we established? That the apostle John, following Scripture’s custom, struck with the word “world” not the nature of things but the vices of wills. And he denied that the desire of the flesh is from God in the same way that he denied this of everything in the world. Manichaeus seized on this, as though following its logic, but according to his own faithlessness rather than the apostle’s meaning. He asserts that neither the desire of the flesh, nor flesh itself, nor, finally, the whole world was made by God. Following him, you believe that the desire of the flesh was created not by God but by the devil.

english: It is therefore established that blessed John gave you no occasion for error, and that you have swallowed what Manichaeus put forward. Now that we have defended the apostle’s reputation, let us briefly come to grips with this point. What do you think Saint John means here when he declares that the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes are not from God? Does he mean the very kind of desire that falls into vice not through its permitted moderation but through its forbidden excess? Or does he mean only the excess, which is found to be voluntary, not natural (compare 1 John 2:16) (1 John 2:16)?

english: If you say that the name “desire” (1 John 2:16) includes even that measure in which it experiences the lawful pleasure of natural things, so that the desire of the flesh seems condemned in its entirety, then profess that the sense of sight, the world itself, and everything in the world were created by the devil. For all are equally said not to be from God. If you agree to that, you will certainly not become a Manichaean, since you already are one. You will simply show it by your confession, as you long ago showed it by your arguments. But if, frightened at having your error exposed, you say that under the names “desire of the flesh,” “desire of the eyes,” and “world” the apostle did not condemn the things themselves—which are harmless when they remain within permitted limits, and become blameworthy when they run into forbidden territory—then the point I argued in my first work will be clear: neither the kind, nor the form, nor the proper measure of natural desire is blameworthy, but only its excess. Therefore have the decency to leave this apostolic testimony alone from now on. If you pollute it with even a passing mention, you will be shown to have gained no defense at all, while being publicly exposed (compare 1 John 2:16).

english: I treated this passage in the second book of my earlier work and showed that the desire of the flesh, which stirs the appeal of taste and sight, existed in the human being before guilt did (compare Genesis 3:6) (Genesis 3:6).

added_allusions.reason: The appeal to taste and sight before the first sin recalls the tree’s attractiveness.

english: Here, however, I must demand to know what dreams revealed to you that the name “desire” should mean the lust of those having intercourse. Without surrendering the resources of truth that a long discussion has disclosed, let us suppose it has not yet become clear that the flesh’s sensations belong to the same author as its form.

Even if we pretend that this is uncertain, the thickest cloud of doubt will immediately envelop you. For this phrase, “desire of the flesh,” contains absolutely no indication of the reproductive organs. I can therefore say that this expression strikes at ears thirsting for different songs; I can say that Saint John rebukes the glutton’s palate; I can say that he blames nostrils dying for perfumes. In short, I can say anything except what you suppose. The choice is open when no specific word imposes a restriction. Either deny, then, that people desire the things I have named, and contradict everyone’s awareness, as you usually do; or, if your shamelessness has not yet hardened enough to resist these facts, admit that a condemnation of sexual pleasure is not found even in the words.

What help, then, can you gain from my unwillingness, amid discussion of the union of the sexes and the fertility of those who join together, to disparage it by the name of desire? Neither you nor Manichaeus has been able to prove that it is devilish. And the very sequence of the preceding argument had already made it clear that this sensation, which affects the bodies of those who unite, goes back to the work of the same one whose institution accounts for bodies, marriages, and seeds.

After my first work, published to the holy Turbantius, there should be no need to discuss the necessary modesty surrounding natural functions. The matter was handled there so fully that no uncertainty about it can arise unless people abandon their minds altogether.

Yet since the defender of inherited sin cannot move even a fingernail’s breadth away from it, and wears out my modesty with his rhetorical elegance over why the act of sexual union itself pleases different people, I choose to settle these points with the brevity appropriate to matters already treated. Both here and in passages below, where I said, “For this reason a man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24) (Genesis 3:7), and added that the prophet came close to endangering modesty in order to express faithfully what took place, he is delighted, as though he had found plunder. He exults and cries: “An entirely open confession, forced out by the power of truth! Let the reason be given why the prophet came close to endangering modesty when expressing God’s works. Can it really be that human works should cause no shame but be openly gloried in, while divine works are shameful? Can it really be that, when God’s works are spoken of and expressed, the prophet’s love or labor wins no honor, but his modesty is endangered? What could God have done that his spokesman would be ashamed to say? More seriously, should a human being be ashamed of some work that God, not man, has done in man, when all craftsmen labor and strive as much as they can not to be ashamed of their works? Surely what shames us is what shamed those first human beings when they covered their private parts (compare Genesis 3:7). It is the punishment of sin, the wound and trace of sin, the lure and fuel of sin, the law in our members fighting against the law of the mind (compare Romans 7:23). This causes shame, and rightly causes shame. For if this were not so, what could be more ungrateful or irreligious than for us to be ashamed in our members, not of our own fault or punishment, but of God’s works?” (Romans 7:23) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.9.22).

His delight is certainly clear. He cannot put a bridle on his joy. He has hold of a statement of mine by which he thinks he can show that natural desire is evil and assign it to the devil’s works. He says that this statement was forced from my mouth by the power of truth, and proclaims that it is utterly wicked and profane if we acknowledge that things we say were made by God must be covered out of modesty. But, carried away by his excitement, he could not weigh what he was saying. He asserts that there is nothing shameful in God’s works, but that the activity of the reproductive organs is shameful and therefore cannot be assigned to the Creator’s works. Then suddenly he confesses that it was assigned to our bodies not only honorably but justly, not only by God creating but even by God judging! I showed in the third book of my earlier work that the same thing cannot be both punishment and guilt.

Law in the members fights the law of the mind.

translator_notes: The opening sentence is syntactically awkward in the supplied Latin. The translation connects its question about pleasure to Augustine’s attack on Julian’s modesty; the relation of these clauses is uncertain.

english: There is therefore no need to labor over this. Still, I commend the disputant’s sharpness: what he says was imposed by God as punishment, he refuses to say was created by God. He pronounces incompatible with God’s works what he wants to be compatible with God’s judgments.

So there is no shame in his works, but the greatest ugliness in his sentences! Guilt certainly deserves punishment. But does the disgrace due to guilt therefore pass into the punishment, so that what the guilty person did can be named without shame, while what God did in judging cannot be spoken of without dishonor?

It is nevertheless clear that my accuser is rolling in the very mud he recoils from. For he has invented the claim that the punishment of lust was justly imposed, and insists that this justice belongs to the divine sentence. Yet he does not deny that the pronouncement of the sentence is God’s work. He says lust, which he admits is shameful, arose from that sentence. He has therefore brought back into God’s work the very shame he had driven away.

As though to crown this with a wickedness all his own, he added that God inflicted a punishment that was a lure and fuel for sin: a law in our members fighting unconquered against the law of our mind (compare Romans 7:23). By this sort of vengeance God would multiply crimes, not punish them. Having been angry at the evil will by which the sin was committed, he would make sinning a necessity thereafter. Let Manichaean frenzy decide what kind of judgment this is. At least it is clear that this judge invented by Augustine only pretends to abhor sin. In reality, he clings to sins with such affection that they could not find a more attentive nurse (Romans 7:23).

added_allusions.reason: The law in the members fights the law of the mind.

english: What, then, do you mean, most subtle disputant? Is modesty about God’s works sacrilegious, because everything God has made must be done openly, lest our hesitation seem to accuse the craftsman? Then the apostle Paul was wrong when he described God’s works and said, “Our less respectable parts receive greater honor; and God arranged the body, giving more abundant honor to the part that lacked it, so that there should be no division in the body” (1 Corinthians 12:23–25).

Then respectable people are also wrong to take care to screen natural functions with modesty. So you yourself should evacuate the remains of your food—which you certainly admit do not belong to lust—under the people’s eyes. Indeed, to lend your doctrine authority by your example, perform in church everything you say happens at the will’s command. Be content to hide only the act of sexual union, from which you long ago abstained by resolution and perhaps now also through old age. Say that it is a great sacrilege for anything whose creator is God to avoid public view. Eat, then, in the marketplace or in the meeting places where your arguments resound. And when clothes become a burden under a scorching sun, cover only that part of your body that the devil has moved, and walk about otherwise naked. For you pronounce it ungrateful and profane to cover anything assigned to God’s works. Since you do none of these things—unless further progress has already brought you to do them—your very conduct confirms one of two conclusions: either everything you do not perform in public view belongs to the devil, or your doctrine has fallen, on the testimony, if not of your heart, at least of your belly.

These are foolish matters, which insult my pen more than they burden it. Yet they follow necessarily from your belief. Still, I again urge the reader to pay attention. You tried to assert that whatever is proved to be God’s work is not shameful. Though you could not establish that, you committed yourself most clearly to this: you would remove shame from lust if it were shown to be God’s work. I proved this so thoroughly in my first work that I do not think even you will doubt it once you read it. Nevertheless, since this invention of yours indicates that those books have not yet reached your hands, I will not shrink from demonstrating the same point here as well.

Who, then, do you think created the irrational animals? At certain seasons they are stirred by the most ardent lust, so that it even sharpens each species’ ferocity: “Then the boar is savage, then the tigress most cruel”; “Above all, the frenzy of mares is remarkable” (Virgil, Georgics 3.248, 266). In spring the grasses swell; in spring an abundance of tender moisture overflows; “And the herds seek mating on their appointed days” (compare Virgil, Georgics 2.324–331). It would take too long to go through them one by one. Every kind of creature—held aloft by flight, submerged by swimming, or scattered by wandering through air, sea, or woods, yet neither raised by reason nor lowered by guilt—is inflamed by the familiar pleasure of bodily union. Did they receive the sexual ardor they experience through God’s work or the devil’s? You will undoubtedly cry out: God’s. So God kindles sex with natural pleasure. Manichaeus, to be sure, denies this more consistently than you do.

For the man from whom you learned to condemn the desire of the flesh considered what he must say. He pursues wherever he can find it the thing he had defined as devilish and removed from God’s works. Thus, through desire he assigned human bodies to the devil as their author, and through human beings he assigned all living creatures to him. But you still remain in Manichaeus’s camp and carry his largest dragon standard, from which you breathe deadly poison into unhappy minds by teaching natural evil and the criminality of marriage. Yet you refuse to hurl the weapons your teacher supplied against all natures. Friendlier to the beasts—though you spare them only to accuse the condition of rational creatures with greater authority—you agree that God made in their bodies what the devil made in ours, although you admit that the same thing exists in human beings more mildly than in animals.

Let the thoughtful reader understand what has been established. You do not deny that God made bodily lust in animals. This feeling is therefore not unworthy of God’s works, since it is found more strongly in substances that have taken nothing of the devil’s evil, not even by the slightest act of will. Desire, then, is defended by the example of animals and by the dignity of its author. What God, the maker of bodies, made, and what a nature free of sin possesses, is neither evil nor devilish. Once this is clear, I ask whether you agree that God made the lust experienced by human bodies. If you agree, the dispute is over: you will be corrected and Manichaeus will remain crushed. But if you say, “It could not have been made by God in human bodies,” I reply that you consider this pleasure and desire of the flesh unworthy of human works, not God’s. There can be no doubt: if you acknowledge something was made by God somewhere, yet say it could not have been made in human beings, you are not taking away the testimony due to desire but seeking an undeserved distinction for the human body.

See, then, how profane your sect’s conclusion is. You call unworthy of mortal flesh what was not unworthy of the Creator’s work. By this reasoning you have not disparaged lust; you have exalted the human being you meant to accuse. Such is the consistency, and such the reward, of someone who declares war on truth: he is always struck by results opposite to his efforts. I will therefore now rise against you with a more consistent use of your own words, as every sensible person recognizes. Can it be that when God’s works are assessed and described, reason receives no hearing and the examples of all natures receive no consideration (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.9.22)? Does human madness rise so high that a man thinks unsuitable for his own flesh what he sees flourishing through God’s work in creatures that share his nature? For the origin and constitution of our bodies are no different from those of these creatures.

Just as we received God’s image through the reason of the mind (compare Genesis 1:26–27), so we experience our kinship with cattle through the affinity of the flesh. Although its form differs, its substance, drawn from the material of the elements, is one. Our flesh will indeed see eternity according to the merits of the rational soul: either miserable in suffering or glorious in rewards (Genesis 1:26–27).

added_allusions.reason: Humankind bears God’s image.

english: On what grounds, then, would something be unworthy, not of God’s image—for the soul’s substance differs from the flesh’s—but of the perishable servant of God’s image, when it was not unworthy of God himself to create it? God made bodies; God distinguished their sexes; God made the reproductive organs; God implanted the feeling through which these bodies unite; God also gave power to seeds; God works in nature’s hidden places from the material of seeds. But God makes nothing evil and nothing guilty.

God made the lust of human beings just as he made that of animals. In animals he left the impulses unrestrained, but in rational human beings God established a limit. The prudence and decency God gave provide desire with a covering. Therefore God blames neither its proper measure nor its kind, but its excess. That excess arises from the unruliness of free will and accuses not nature’s condition but what the agent deserves.

Now consider what follows from your opinion: whatever is believed good should not be covered out of modesty. But I have shown that this desire naturally implanted in the sexes is not evil, since it belongs to God’s work. Accordingly, you must abandon either your impiety or your modesty. But why do I say this? “If the Ethiopian changes his skin or the leopard its spots” (Jeremiah 13:23), then you too will be washed clean of the Manichaean mysteries.

It follows, then, that you must put aside modesty and, while remaining friends with your teacher, enter an alliance with the Cynics. As Cicero reports in On Duties, the arguments of some Stoics also accompany them. They criticize ordinary decency because we regard as disgraceful in speech things that are not shameful in reality, while we call by their proper names things that are shameful in reality. Committing robbery, perpetrating fraud, and committing adultery are shameful acts, but naming them is not obscene. Working to produce children is honorable in reality but obscene in name. “They argue many other things,” he says, “against modesty along these lines. But let us follow nature and avoid everything that offends the approval of eyes and ears” (Cicero, On Duties, book 1).

So you too, who dislike this natural reasoning, the sister of decency, must either say that working to produce children—a task that requires modesty—is uglier and more profane than robbery, sacrilege, and murder of a parent, all of which are supremely shameful in reality but contain no obscenity in their names; or, if you blush to accuse marriage so far that it outweighs even crimes when compared with them, urge married couples to name that union as confidently and freely as we usually name murder of a parent or robbery. If you then add, to mock Christian ears as you usually do, that bodily union intended for offspring is stained by no injustice but can be judged good within its proper measure, embrace the deed of Crates of Thebes. He was a wealthy and noble man so devoted to the Cynic sect that he left his inherited wealth and moved to Athens with his wife Hipparchia, who followed this philosophy with equal commitment. When he wished to have intercourse with her in public, as Cornelius Nepos relates, she drew her cloak over herself to conceal it and was beaten by her husband. “Plainly,” he said—in keeping with your views—“you are still poorly taught, since you do not dare to do in others’ presence what you know you are right to do” (Cornelius Nepos).

Such conduct is entirely due from your flocks: natural acts should be practiced without any barrier of modesty, because they are proved good by having been created by God for multiplying bodies. Return the favor to the four-footed animals, then. Their examples defend your bodily sensation against the devil’s ownership and Manichaeus’s mouth; you too should imitate their freedom in mating as testimony to the goodness of the act. It is fitting that those who have defended your organs should provide instruction for your conduct.

To establish by repetition what we have done: you said lust should be clothed in no modesty if God had made it. Although I treated this fully in the four books of my earlier work, I have also shown here, through the testimony of all the animals that you still admit were created by God, that sexual lust was created by God. Yet I acknowledge that in human beings it should be screened by modesty. It therefore follows from your doctrine that you should bring back before us the elegance of the Cynics after its long exile and perform natural acts before the city’s eyes, because they were made by God. Do you see how blindly you leaped upon my statement, “In order to express faithfully what took place, the prophet came close to endangering modesty” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.9.22)? Your teacher, whose inventions I quoted in the previous book, criticizes this consistently with his own fables, since he denies that God made any bodies. But you have shamelessly dared to handle it while acknowledging—though out of fear—that God created the bodies whose sensation you attribute to the ruler of darkness. That claim has been crushed with all the power of truth expressed in the evangelist’s faithful words: “Everything was made through God, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

The time urges us to move on to other matters. But since you plainly have nothing to peddle to uneducated ears except modesty about natural functions, I will touch as briefly as possible on what seems to remain. Who denies that the decency with which we cover our genitals varies according to persons, places, occupations, and customs? Thus nakedness that would be quite obscene in public gatherings carries no shame in the baths. The dress of the bedroom is one thing, half-naked and carefree; dress in public is another, more careful and more ample. Again, neglect of precautions often indicates familiarity: the more unknown or honored the person present, the more carefully one dresses. And no one has blamed sailors or many craftsmen for nakedness. To show that such simplicity belongs more to the work than to the person, even the apostle Peter, following everyone’s custom, fished naked in the boat after the Lord’s resurrection (John 21:7). Turn your eyes next to the work of physicians: in their care for health they apply their art to the parts modesty conceals. Nakedness is even becoming to athletes.

Moreover, not only among young people bound together in a wanton companionship, but even among certain whole nations, both sexes go uncovered and unite without choosing a private place. Yet why be surprised if a Scot and the barbarity of neighboring peoples do this, when the philosophy mentioned above judged the same thing acceptable, and the doctrine of the advocates of inherited sin has arrived at the same point? What fixed measure of modesty, what boundary, can be maintained amid so many variations, and amid practices defended partly by necessity and partly by companionship, by which it could be proved that the devil mixed natural ardor into the sexes? Your opinion’s support has plainly been dissolved by occupations, places, customs, arts, and whole nations together. Meanwhile, what I defend through reason itself and the teaching of the apostle Paul remains unconquered: God, the author of all things, created every body, every bodily member, and every bodily sense. But he arranged them so that, as occasions require, modesty should clothe some of our members and natural decency should display others. It would be as indecent to cover these others as to expose the privacy of the genitals at an unsuitable time (compare 1 Corinthians 12:23–25) (1 Corinthians 12:23–25).

added_allusions.reason: Paul’s account of honor and modesty among bodily members.

english: Having settled this in the present work as far as a matter already treated required, I come to your statement that this natural desire was not in Christ. For this is how you object to me: “But amid all these things he was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world. The devil is called the ruler of this world. He did not find this desire in the Lord, because the Lord came among human beings as a man without it” (John 14:30) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.2.5; compare John 14:30). You have therefore pronounced that Christ, whom the catholic faith confesses to be a true human being in every respect, did not have in his flesh the desire spoken of by the apostle John. But John, as his words showed, declares that the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes, together with the whole world, are not from the Father (1 John 2:16). I have explained how this ought to be understood.

added_allusions.reason: The ruler of the world finds nothing in Christ.

english: But you fasten on the very name “desire” and want the sensation of the eyes to have been as absent from Christ’s body as that of his inner parts.

Here, then, I urge the reader to attend with his whole mind. He will see the Apollinarist heresy revived through you, but with a Manichaean addition. For Apollinaris is said at first to have introduced this account of Christ’s incarnation: only a body seemed to have been assumed from human substance, while the divinity itself took the place of a soul. Christ would thus appear to have taken up a human corpse, not a human being. This began to be overturned by the testimony both of reason and of the Gospel. For if he had assumed flesh alone, everything Christ said in calling himself a man whom the Jews persecuted for speaking the truth would necessarily be accused of falsehood, since a human being cannot exist without soul and body together (compare John 8:40). Or again, he had said in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18) (John 8:40). What soul could be laid down if none had been assumed? After being refuted by the authority of such testimonies and by evident reason, Apollinaris devised another claim from which his heresy, still continuing today, arose. He said that Christ did possess a human soul, but lacked bodily sensations; and he pronounced him incapable of being affected by any sins.

added_allusions.reason: Christ describes himself as a man speaking truth whom his hearers seek to kill.

english: He was not, on this account, someone who avoided offenses through the strength of his judgment, but someone who could not feel the desire for vices because his flesh had the advantage of being separated from our sensations.

As the matter shows, such flattery gravely damages the catholic faith. It is not merely unnecessary but profane. By wishing to show something superior in Christ’s body, lest sharing our flesh should diminish it, Apollinaris deprived him of the full possession of natural sensations. He did not see how far the ruin would extend when truth was damaged even by flattery. For an objection raised by the catholics thundered against him: under such a belief, Christ’s saving mysteries would suffer a greater loss than his members. “If,” (Luke 4:2) they said, “Christ was made from David’s seed (Romans 1:3), made from a woman and made under the Law (Galatians 4:4), in order to give us an example, so that we might follow the footsteps of the one who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:21–22), yet he did not put on all the properties of our substance—if he bore either flesh without a soul or a human being without the sensations nature gives us—then he is not shown to have fulfilled the model of an example and a law. What was praiseworthy in despising the enticements of the senses if, through nature’s favor, he was incapable of them? What was remarkable in restraining eyes that did not wander because his flesh kept them from doing so? What was great in turning his nostrils away from enticing scents if they did not know how to receive them? What was astonishing in maintaining strict restraint over meals every day if he could not feel their appeal? Finally, what difficulty was there in fasting for forty days if hunger could not trouble him (compare Matthew 4:2; Luke 4:2)? What reverence did the discipline of ears deserve, receiving only honorable words, if they had an inborn deafness to improper ones? And what glory was there in chastity if manhood, rather than willingness, was absent, and what was thought to arise from strength of mind came from weakness of the members?” (Matthew 4:2)

Christ fasted forty days and hungered.

english: Finally, what prize was there for endurance if the pain of wounds and blows could not reach the soul because the path of sensation was blocked? What, then, did Apollinaris’s flattery achieve? All the beauty of the virtues Christ had embodied was emptied out and withered by undeserved praises of his nature. Stripped of all the splendor of its truth, it exposed the Mediator’s sacred teaching to ridicule. Moreover, he would not merely lose the distinction of his works, being fortunate by birth rather than by virtue: he would also face charges of fraud if he told mortals, “Strive toward the patience of a man who feels nothing, and come through real torments to the virtues of an unreal body that suffers no pain”; or, “Conquer the definite impulses of your own nature and imitate the chastity of someone whom weakness made appear pure.” Certainly nothing more profane or wicked can be imagined than such inventions.

Apollinaris had not actually said all these things. But by making that one pronouncement—that the man Christ lacked the sensations implanted by nature, which fall into vice through excess rather than through use—he received all these replies from the catholics in silence, condemned by his own opinion. For the catholic faith is built by affirming all the things whose denial, or the consequences of whose denial, formed and condemned Apollinaris’s heresy. Judge, then, what verdict should be passed on you. You condemn the union of the sexes like Manichaeus. You separate the nature of Christ’s flesh from the common condition of humanity, according to the Manichaeans. You accuse the desire of the flesh, following the statements of your teacher Manichaeus. You say that sensory desire was not present in Christ’s body, whether according to the Manichaeans or according to the Apollinarists. Yet you want us to call you neither an Apollinarist nor a Manichaean! Still, I yield and grant you a favor; I do not regret being generous. As far as I am concerned, you may avoid appearing a follower of Apollinaris, for he devised the lesser impiety. But you yourself make it impossible for you to be called anything other than a Manichaean.

I showed in the third book of my first work that, if natural sin were believed, one would necessarily and irrefutably have to say that Christ too inherited guilt from Mary’s flesh. You place him under the devil’s power by asserting that the entire substance of human beings belongs to the devil’s jurisdiction.
So, leaving that aside for the present, I demand to know where you have read that Christ was a eunuch by nature.

Although he was born from a virgin as a sign (compare Isaiah 7:14), he did not reject the male sex; rather, he assumed its reality. He was complete in every internal part, complete in body, a true human being, a perfect man, if we believe the apostle Peter’s discourse in Acts (Acts 2:22, 33). He was distinguished by unbroken chastity, guarding both mind and eyes without ever relaxing his heart’s strength. That he accomplished all this by strength of mind, not weakness of flesh, is witnessed by his sleep, food, beard, sweat, labor, cross, and the lance (compare Matthew 8:24; Luke 24:42–43; Isaiah 50:6; Luke 22:44; John 4:6; John 19:18, 34). These testify that the desire of the flesh, mingled with the senses of the whole body, and the reality, soundness, and natural condition of his members were present in him. He did not lack bodily sensations; he ruled them.

This is the ground on which the catholic faith challenges the nations and the Manichaeans: the message of his flesh, like that of his cross, is foolishness to those who perish, but God’s power to those who will be saved (compare 1 Corinthians 1:18). This is how he commended his love toward us (compare Romans 5:8): the Mediator’s devotion assumed everything that Manichaean impiety tears apart. Therefore nothing in my Lord makes me ashamed. I hold fast to the reality of the members he took on for my salvation, so that I may receive the solidity and strength of his example (Isaiah 7:14) (Matthew 8:24) (Luke 24:42–43) (Luke 22:44) (John 4:6) (John 19:18) (John 19:34) (1 Corinthians 1:18) (Romans 5:8).
