english: I proclaim that all his holiness rested on the benefit of his mind, not on an exemption granted to his flesh. In this way nature is defended both by his creation of it and by his assumption of it, and human life is directed by imitation of his virtues. Neither of these two things can be praised without the truth of the other. His sacred work will have as much dignity as his human body has reality; and the defense of his flesh will extend as far as the holiness of his life requires. Conversely, blame of one affects both. As much will be taken from his virtues as is taken from his limbs. If anything is scraped away from the solidity of his substance, all the adornments of his conduct perish; and losses inflicted on the one born return as an insult to the one who suffered. In short, if the substance of his flesh is reduced by removing any natural property, the entire display of virtues vanishes.

I will therefore deny nothing in the members of the Mediator, made from a woman, that is known to be natural (compare Galatians 4:4). And see how different the boundaries of reason and modesty are. The Christian faith is not ashamed to say that Christ had genitals, although we conceal them in ourselves as decently as we can (Galatians 4:4).

added_allusions.reason: The Mediator was made from a woman.

english: Thus nature has prescribed that there are certain things reason, and likewise faith with reverence, may name, though modesty and decency of conduct do not allow them to be exposed to sight. In this way the Teacher of the Nations assigns reality to Christ’s flesh and holiness to his spirit: “Great,” he says, “is the mystery of devotion, which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in this world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). Just as he commended this to be believed as true, so he announced that its opponents would arise at the end of the age. For he immediately continues: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage, requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth; for every creature of God is good” (1 Timothy 4:1–4).

The apostle both foresaw and condemned this pollution of the churches that you vomited out by following Manichaeus: this betrayal by those departing from the faith, which consists in preaching natural evil and condemning marital union. He showed not only what would be said, but also what would follow from it.
translator_notes: The source note cites only 1 Timothy 4:4, but the quotation begins at 4:1; the full range is supplied.

english: When he says that abstinence from foods will be taught, an intelligent reader understands that he is not accusing Christian restraint or announcing the possible appearance of people who prescribe the ordeal of fasting (compare 1 Timothy 4:1–4). Rather, he shows that people would arise who said that all the animals God created for mortals’ food were polluted by the devil’s evil because they were born through desire and sexual union. He then expressed the consequence: foods must be renounced if their reproduction is believed devilish. That is why you remove this slander against bodily union from animals, so that your pretense can survive. Yet you say that human beings, made in God’s image, belong to the demon’s jurisdiction because of this very desire in those who beget them (compare Genesis 1:26–27). Both you and Manichaeus therefore have one reason for disparaging substances and transferring them to the devil. But he condemns every animal because of this feeling experienced in a natural act; you condemn not all, but—what is uglier—the better ones. You acquit pigs, dogs, and donkeys to appear to avoid the Manichaeans. But for the very same reason as Manichaeus you condemn all human beings, who were made in God’s image. Placing natural evil nowhere except in God’s image, you declaim against us as accuser of the saints and defender of donkeys (1 Timothy 4:1–4) (Genesis 1:26–27).

added_allusions.reason: Continues interpreting the preceding quotation about forbidding marriage and foods.
Humans made in God’s image.

english: Christ, then, no less a true human being than true God, lacked nothing natural. But it was right that the one giving the example of perfection should excel in every pursuit of virtue. His chastity, exalted by uninterrupted integrity and stirred by no lustful appetite, had remained virgin in its holy mind. His greatness of soul mastered every sense and conquered pain. Through his humanity it was to become imitable by all the faithful, and through its sublimity, wonderful.

So here, as in everything, you have spoken most profanely in saying that what belongs to human nature was absent from Christ’s flesh. You drew this, deceived, not from any sound vein of Scripture but solely from Manichaean filth. Yet to display a greater abundance of resources for defending truth, let us grant your dream that the desire of the flesh you speak of was absent from Christ. This was certainly condemned first in Manichaean and afterward in Apollinarist frenzy. But what support could it give your doctrine? It would not immediately follow that something was evil if he had chosen not to assume it. Since good things rise by degrees in worth, one could say that he proceeded through the best without condemning goods placed below him by choosing those above. Just as he did not defame marriage by following virginity, so he would not have condemned the sensation of the reproductive flesh even if he had been unwilling to possess its capacity in his own substance.

To confirm a plain matter by an example: it is better to possess reason than not to possess it. Human beings were made rational, while animals were made irrational. Yet because human nature surpasses four-footed animals, those animals must not therefore be called an evil or the devil’s work. Suppose, then, that when Christ formed his own members, he chose not to mingle with them a sensation of the reproductive organs that he would not use. When he formed the members of Isaac, Jacob, and everyone else, giving them both sex and sensation, was he therefore doing something evil? Or did he call the devil to help when he came to these things, so that the devil might mingle necessary pleasures into the members Christ himself had assembled? As I have shown, with God’s help, both in this work and in the earlier one, you have obtained absolutely nothing, however small, against the divine works through the person of Christ. For it has become clear that the Savior’s body lacked nothing belonging to human nature.
Accordingly, there can be no sin in that nature, since no injustice was found in the one in whom the whole nature is present (compare 1 Peter 2:22) (1 Peter 2:22).

added_allusions.reason: No sin found in Christ, continuing the quotation at §49.

english: Therefore, whether sexual desire was or was not in Christ’s flesh, it is not shown to be evil or devilish.

I hurry toward other matters, yet astonishment at these things holds me fast. What is this great fury against another person, that even if you do not understand Scripture, you fail to weigh your own words? You always argue in such a way that whatever you throw returns upon you with greater force. You said, of course, that there is no cause of modesty except the desire of the flesh displayed in movements of the reproductive organs.

You also said that it is sacrilege to judge anything believed to have been made by God shameful, apart from this desire of the flesh; and that Christ did not have this desire of the flesh, which gives mortals a reason for modesty. Did you not see what follows? Christ should have joined gatherings naked, without any regard for modesty, so as not to incur the sacrilege you invent by being ashamed, in his flesh that had no desire, of his own and his Father’s works. But if he had no such desire and nevertheless observed modesty, then even on your account it is irrefutably proved that modesty is due to the human body, not to its sexual heat.

You therefore see that you vainly called it a sin to acknowledge that a covering must be applied to these works God made: our Lord instituted this as humanity’s maker and practiced it when he became human. May reverence for the Redeemer grant pardon because, to defend the truth of the mystery and destroy the Manichaeans’ wickedness, I speak boldly of his flesh. Unless faith demanded it, restrained reverence would not touch this subject.

“But he,” you say, “was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh. He is silent because he is ashamed; and with a remarkable shamelessness of shame, if one may say so, he is ashamed to name what he is not ashamed to praise” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.7.17). So you are displeased that we know, according to the apostle, that our less respectable parts must be covered with the decency they require (1 Corinthians 12:23). In this, our judgment follows the Creator’s: what he placed in a private part of the body, we likewise cover with a modest screen.

The varieties of expression whose service I use, and which you not only fail to imitate but even attack, were developed by refinement in Greek and Latin, not in every language. Other languages are called natural because subsequent cultivation has brought them neither richness nor polish; they use entirely simple names for bodily parts. Thus among the Hebrews, in whose language Scripture’s purity is contained, everything is indicated by its own proper word.

The genitals of both sexes are named as freely as feet and knees. Yet even with this authority supporting me, I have not neglected the aids of more modest speech. Neglect of decency without any compulsion from the subject lies open to the most just criticism. Decency should be maintained in words no less than in actions, as far as the subject allows. Natural desire, then, could not be convicted by the reproach of shame and has been defended by its Creator’s dignity. The purpose was not to treat it as some great good, since it is shared by human beings and animals, but as a necessary instrument of the sexes: rescued from the demons’ jurisdiction and placed among the works of the one who made the world and bodies. No one accuses it except Manichaeus and his heir, the advocate of inherited sin. It is therefore evident that the entire fiction of natural sin has vanished, since its whole support depended on accusations against nature.

I therefore had to ask what the devil recognized as his own in the sexes, by which he could rightfully pluck their fruit. He had not assembled the flesh, formed the members, given the reproductive organs, distinguished sex, or ordained marriage. Nor had he honored with fertility or sprinkled with pleasure the union without which marriage cannot exist.

Trying to meet these arguments with a deer’s fear and a fox’s deceit, you deceived the patron to whom you write by telling him that the ruler of darkness dominates God’s works and image because of natural bodily sensation, that is, the desire of the flesh (compare Genesis 1:26–27). Yet the flesh’s sensation must necessarily belong to the same author as the flesh’s nature (Genesis 1:26–27).

added_allusions.reason: Human beings are God’s image.

english: It is therefore clear that you did not strive to refute the objections, but to deceive miserably the patron to whom you were writing. You wanted him to think you had brought forward some crude statement that you could rightly bite at, although you had already praised it by conceding the preceding points and the divine institution of bodies.

I admit, however, that you thought very hard about what to say. Your talent and your effort are evident. You certainly weighed most skillfully what should be asserted on behalf of inherited sin. No one else could have written more cleverly for natural evil. Indeed, even you could not have accomplished it so elegantly had your old teacher’s inventions not helped your talent.

For you understood that a charge could never be fastened on infants, who have deserved nothing of their own, without condemning bodies. You therefore needed the help of Manichaeus, who excluded the desire of the flesh from God’s works and assigned both marriage and bodies themselves to the devil as their author.

So the ugliness of the cause you defend has made truth rout you and drive you away. Otherwise, if you wished to come over to the catholics, how much more elegantly and fully you yourself would develop what I assert!
Although I hardly dare pronounce you gifted with a sharp and watchful mind, when I see how sluggish and ugly your judgment is in choosing the cause you have undertaken.

For if, with your faith entirely intact, you were attempting to shake what cannot be defeated merely to show the strength of your learning, in the manner of a school exercise, while intending to award the victory to those you opposed once the playful contest ended, I would approve your literary enthusiasm but rebuke your irreligious example. Instead, you follow with the ugliest stubbornness a doctrine that lacks even the false coloring of plausibility and that you cannot defend by any testimonies of the Law, since these never count against reason. It bristles with impiety and lies prostrate in foolishness, existing nowhere except amid the groins of human desires, pierced through by decency, argument, and sacred law. One of three conclusions therefore follows: either your understanding is leaden, or you suffer the chains of that sorcery we have heard is contained in the Manichaean mysteries, or both at once.

I, however, find nothing to admire in my own talent because I understand that sin cannot exist without will, bodies without God, bodily sensations without bodies, marriage without union, or newborn people without God’s activity. And I hold as certain that what is proved unjust is not divine, and what is divine cannot be proved unjust. It is no less plain than these things that imputing one person’s sins to others who were not even there, much less consenting, is unjust. Enlightened by these suns, I am entirely justified in looking down on the Manichaeans’ caves. They think either that sin can exist without will, or that God does not make human beings, or that bodily sensation belongs to one author and bodies to another. They suppose either that someone weighed down by charges of injustice is God, or that the eternal creator of all can be charged with the crime of injustice, or that even a shadow of justice remains when one person’s acts of will are attached to another person’s birth. Accordingly, I assess the merits of the opposing sides by their causes, not by their talents.

But let us return to the case. You said I had been unwilling to name desire because “it is not from the Father but from the world. The devil is called the ruler of this world. He did not find it in the Lord, because the Lord came among human beings as a man without it” (1 John 2:16) (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.26.41; compare 1 John 2:16; John 14:30). Notice this: you were speaking of a natural thing, and after saying it was from the world, you added that the devil should be believed ruler of the whole world. You were thus acknowledging him as author not of voluntary acts but of natural things—that is, of natures (John 14:30) (1 John 2:16; John 14:30).

added_allusions.reason: Desire of flesh is from the world, not the Father.
The ruler of the world finds nothing in Christ.

english: After saying this, you added: “Hence the Lord himself also says, ‘See, the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me’” (John 14:30). Then you add your own explanation: “Nothing, that is, of sin, either inherited at birth or added in the course of life.” Show, then, that the Lord said in the Gospel that he had no sin inherited at birth.

Why do you deceive unhappy souls by lying that something was indicated when it was not? The Lord says in the Gospel: “See, the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John 14:30) (Matthew 4:1–11). The devil certainly encountered no sin in him, because he was defeated in every temptation he brought against him, whether when he hungered or afterward when he preached, through his persecutors (compare Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13). The Savior therefore declares that the devil detected no sin in him. Yet he certainly would have found it if anything were inherited through the flesh’s condition, since Christ too had been made from a woman descended from David’s seed and Adam’s stock (compare Galatians 4:4; Romans 1:3; Luke 3:23–38) (Luke 4:1–13) (Galatians 4:4) (Romans 1:3) (Luke 3:23–38).

added_allusions.reason: The devil tempts Christ while hungry.
The devil tempts Christ while hungry.
Christ made from a woman.
Christ from David’s seed.
Christ’s ancestry traced to Adam.

english: The devil would therefore have found a natural crime in him if any such crime existed. He would have held the body liable if he had poisoned it either in the first parent or in the very woman who bore him. It would not matter whether a late and ineffective intention of the will resisted the conditions of its own material. Struggling against nature, it would not cleanse the one born but would provoke the tyrant—all the more since the will could not be free if nature were captive. So if sin lay in the very sensation and condition of the flesh, if human nature itself belonged to the demon’s dominion, Christ would either have been guilty or would not have been human. If, then, a curse is assigned to human nature, the one who became flesh to dwell among us must likewise either be assigned guilt or be deprived of humanity (compare John 1:14) (John 1:14).

added_allusions.reason: The Word became flesh to dwell among us.

english: Manichaeus did both. Having invented the claim that evil exists naturally in flesh, he said that there was no flesh in Christ, to avoid confessing that there was injustice in him.

But the catholic faith crushed him on both points. It declares that evil does not exist naturally in flesh and that therefore Christ lacked nothing human and possessed nothing unjust. Conscious of his own saving work, he cries: “See, the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John 14:30). Certainly nothing he could accuse: he could not defame a nature whose will he had not bent toward sins.

That was the very reason he tempted Christ: following his customary art, he wanted to capture him by persuasion, since he could corrupt no one by creating him (compare Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13) (Matthew 4:1–11) (Luke 4:1–13).

added_allusions.reason: The temptation of Christ.
The temptation of Christ.

english: Thus Christ’s incarnation defends the work of his own divinity. He brought to me my nature and his own will, offering that will as a mirror and a rule for me. By declaring that the devil had found no sin in him, he showed that guilt is acquired not from the flesh’s creation but solely from the will (compare John 14:30). Nowhere in Scripture do we read that Christ escaped a sin he knew was inherited at birth. Rather, clear testimony fully teaches that the righteousness of the humanity he assumed rested not on a difference of nature but on voluntary action (John 14:30).

added_allusions.reason: The devil finds no sin in Christ.

english: For the apostle Peter says: “Christ died for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:21–22). The apostle’s statement certainly agrees with the Lord’s voice. The Lord says in the Gospel, “The ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John 14:30). The teacher of the Church commends the same point, saying there was no offense in Christ. But by truthful testimony he explains why Christ had no sin: “Because,” he says, “he committed no sin.” He did not say, “Because he received no sin,” but, “Because he committed no sin.”
translator_notes: The source note gives 1 Peter 2:21; the quotation continues into 2:22. Julian’s “died” is retained rather than replaced by “suffered”.

english: But if there were a crime in nature, Peter’s statement would have been ignorant. He evidently judged it sufficient testimony to spotless holiness to clear Christ’s actions of crimes, although sin would be believed to dwell in him through natural poison. If Peter had thought anything of natural evil, he would therefore have mentioned this part more carefully and emphatically. He would have written, “Christ left us an example: he neither committed sin nor acquired the sin we inherit at birth.” (1 Peter 2:21–22) Then it could fittingly follow that no deceit was found in his mouth (compare 1 Peter 2:21–22). But if Peter had thought this, he would never have mentioned an example. For whom would he have presented for human beings to imitate if the nature of an alien flesh had set Christ apart, and a difference of substance had impeached the authority of his teaching?

added_allusions.reason: Explicit repeated biblical wording or explanation of the same passage in the ongoing argument; the cross-reference identifies the passage, not an exact modern translation.

english: Moreover, the belief in natural sin would not merely destroy the force of imitation; it would expose fraud in the very praise offered to Christ. With what seriousness, with what face, could anyone say that no deceit was found in his mouth? If he had come in a condition of flesh different from ours, he would be proved to have practiced deliberate deceit not only in teaching, which is less serious, but even in being born, which is more serious. What sort of conduct would this be? Human beings would be established in natural evil and the devil’s kingdom, sinning under the deadly necessity of an inborn plague, or naturally serving the law of sin that ruled in their members (compare Romans 7:23). Yet he would force them, even under threat of punishment, to imitate him, and demand his own righteousness from people of a flesh whose evil had terrified him so greatly that, though he wished to display a model of goodness under its appearance, he avoided the reality of its nature. How much more rightly could the sickness of sinners, secure in their claim to be compelled, say to him: “When we are well, we all give sound advice to the sick. If you were in this condition, you would think very, very differently!” (Romans 7:23)

What, then, has your impiety achieved? This necessary consequence: if sin is believed naturally present in our flesh, Christ either assumed that flesh and is liable to its evil, or did not assume it and is bound inescapably by the injustice, not of his birth, which then appears false, but of deliberate deception. All this is so foul with blasphemy that it can scarcely be set out without horror, even while being torn apart. Let the Mediator’s dignity therefore stand by his example and his work, and by our faith. Defending the truth through both his words and his apostle’s, that faith never ceases to proclaim that Christ, a true human being, assumed from Mary’s womb flesh of the same nature as ours. Though a true human being in every respect, he had no sin. To indicate this, it suffices for the apostle Peter to say that he committed no sin, teaching that one who had not committed it could not possess it (compare 1 Peter 2:21–22). No deceit was found in his mouth. He offered a holy example to those sharing his nature, which he himself had made in everyone. Sin is therefore clearly not inborn, since Christ did not have it: without losing the honor of his divinity, he became flesh precisely so that we could imitate him (1 Peter 2:21–22).

added_allusions.reason: The law of sin in bodily members.
Christ’s example, absence of sin, and absence of deceit.

translator_notes: The speech about healthy people advising the sick echoes Terence, The Woman of Andros, 309–310; it is a literary comparison, not a saying of Christ.

english: Having completed these points as the subject required, I would like to question you at least briefly. With what confidence do you say there was no sin in Christ while praising Jerome’s writings? In that Dialogue he composed under the names Atticus and Critobulus, with a remarkable elegance befitting such a faith, he even relies on the testimony of a fifth Gospel, which he says he translated, to try to show that Christ had not only natural but even voluntary sin, because of which he knew he needed cleansing by John’s baptism (compare Jerome, Dialogue against the Pelagians 3.1). From another testimony of John the evangelist, he also fastens on Christ the disgrace of falsehood (compare Jerome, Dialogue against the Pelagians 2.6; John 7:8–10). In the letter you sent to Alexandria, you boast of this work so much that you say Pelagius, overwhelmed by its masses of Scripture, cannot defend free choice. But that work was answered by the catholic man who had been attacked. I have now mentioned it only to make you recognize that you agree neither with the holy Scriptures nor even with the helpers of your own doctrine (John 7:8–10).

added_allusions.reason: The charge concerns Christ’s words about going up to the feast, discussed in Jerome’s Dialogue.

translator_notes: Julian is making accusations against Jerome here; these are not statements by the translator about Jerome’s teaching. The “fifth Gospel” is the Gospel according to the Hebrews quoted by Jerome. The source locators are retained; in the NPNF English arrangement the baptism passage is Dialogue 3.2 and the feast passage is 2.17. See https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/30113.htm and https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/30112.htm.

english: For you abandon the Manichaeans when they disparage pigs and goats, though you accompany them in accusing human nature. With them, too, you overthrow in Christ not the appearance of flesh but the basis of his example. At least in words, you also remove natural sin from Christ, lest you seem to place him too under the devil’s power, something not even Manichaeus himself did. Yet you praise Jerome, who does not fear to blaspheme him by saying that he entered into familiarity even with voluntary crimes. So you roll without turning aside among your friends’ various filth and inventions, and rage in abuse only against the catholics. For they say that God is not the author of evil; that human beings made by him are not naturally evil; that God’s laws are just; that his image can turn away from evil and do good (compare Genesis 1:26–27; Psalm 34:14); and that Christ committed no sin in his members, his commands, or his judgments (compare 1 Peter 2:22). Therefore, although the assertion of truth makes you sick, I believe that thoughtful people are instructed, and even some of those wounded by your lies can be healed (Genesis 1:26–27) (Psalm 34:14) (1 Peter 2:22).

added_allusions.reason: Humans bear God’s image.
Turn away from evil and do good.
Christ committed no sin.
This verse repeats the cited psalm’s command to turn from evil and do good.

translator_notes: “Turn away from evil and do good” corresponds to modern Psalm 34:14, LXX Psalm 33:15, and is repeated in 1 Peter 3:11.

english: Enough of these matters. Let us now come to the point on which a large part of the case turns. Examined and drained of life by its force, the Manichaeans’ envoy has produced evidence of a reply as faithful as his talent is elegant. After praising and approving the words of mine I quoted above, with nothing new intervening, he approached the part in which the argument I had promised was completed. I had asked through what those whom God made were under the devil. I answered in his name, “Through sin, not through nature,” and replied in my own: “But, as you yourself agree, just as offspring cannot exist without the sexes, so an offense cannot exist without will. Do infants, then, possess a will at the time of conception, when they do not yet possess a soul? Or at the time of their birth, when they do not yet possess the use of reason?”

When he reached this point, he set out only this much of my objection: “But just as offspring cannot exist without the sexes, so an offense cannot exist without will.” And he replied: “Indeed, that is so. For in this way ‘through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12). Through that one man’s evil will, all sinned in him, when all were that one man. For that reason, each inherited original sin from him” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15).

I therefore urge the reader to examine our contest attentively. What did you gain, most learned of two-footed creatures, by failing to complete my statement? Although the part you suppressed contained an explanation of the earlier statement, the whole force nevertheless remains equally in what you put before yourself. I faithfully set out your usual reply, as your own assent made clear. Asking through what infants whom God made were under the devil, I answered in your place, “Through sin, not through nature.” You certainly see that I practiced no deceit here. I said what is on the advocate of inherited sin’s lips, although it is not in his doctrine. To this I replied, “But just as offspring cannot exist without the sexes, so an offense cannot exist without will.”

You broke this apart with shameless deceit. You mentioned my words that, just as offspring cannot exist without the sexes, so an offense cannot exist without will; but you suppressed what followed about the infants’ will. And you answer, “Indeed, that is so. For in this way ‘through one man sin entered the world’ (Romans 5:12): through that one man’s evil will, all sinned in him.” Is this answering? Is this arguing? Is this, finally, even showing a regard for sobriety? Learned people certainly laugh at the cleverness of sophisms, where shared words are used to trick the respondent’s simplicity. Yet those sophisms, though lacking the solidity of truth, are at least colored by an elegant surface. What sort of monstrosity of argument is this, which is neither solid with truth nor polished with sophistry? I certainly said that sin cannot exist without free will. Once that is granted, your doctrine is destroyed, since you think an offense exists in human nature without any will on the part of those held guilty.
translator_notes: Romans 5:12 retains the Latin “in whom all sinned”, the wording being debated.

english: With what shamelessness, then, do you both approve my statement and refuse to abandon your doctrine? The statements of the two sides cannot be joined by any agreement, since opposite assertions do not share the truth at the same time. If I agreed that sin was natural, I would necessarily fall away from the force of the statement that sin can exist only in free will. In the same way, you, by agreeing that I spoke rightly in declaring that no sin exists without will, should immediately have rejected the opinion by which you believed sin to be natural.
For it is evident that whatever is natural is not voluntary.

Therefore, if sin is natural, it is not voluntary; if it is voluntary, it is not inborn. These two definitions are as opposed to one another as necessity and will, whose affirmation arises from the denial of the other. Just as “voluntary” means nothing other than “not compelled,” so “compelled” means nothing other than “not voluntary.” These two therefore cannot exist, or as it were live, together. Their nature is such that one lives only when the other is extinguished.

Since this is so unshakable that no argument can overthrow it, choose whichever you prefer and consistently affirm either my statement or yours, so that you impute guilt either to necessity or to will. When I say “whichever you prefer,” I am not advising you as though your opinion were still hidden: you learned through Manichaeus to bring crimes into nature. I give this warning so that the truthfulness of your argument may be put on record.

Let the thoughtful and attentive hearer weigh what you answered me. We are certainly discussing infants, who possess no will of their own minds. The question is through what they are under the devil, when God made them and you agree that they themselves have done nothing evil. You proclaimed that they belong to the demon’s jurisdiction because of sin, not because of nature. My reply rose against this: “But just as offspring cannot exist without the sexes, so an offense cannot exist without will.” (Romans 5:12) You answered, “Indeed, that is so”—that is, an offense cannot exist without will. But after confirming this, with what shamelessness did you add, “Yet through one man sin entered the world, through that one man’s will” (compare Romans 5:12)?

added_allusions.reason: Sin entered through one man.

english: Had you been asked about Adam’s actions, or whether he sinned by his will? That question will indeed soon be put against you. Granted, you enjoy deceiving others; but how ugly it is to deceive yourself! Yet I cannot persuade myself that you suffer such ugliness from conviction rather than fraud. In one and the same line you agree that an offense cannot exist without will, then immediately add that the sin which you said could not subsist without a free movement of mind reigns in all human beings without will.

Again, there is a large difference between the propositions. You said, “There is no offense without will,” and answered, “But there is an offense through one person’s will.” Does the following reply, introduced by a preposition taking the accusative case, agree with the earlier definition, secured by a preposition taking the ablative case? The question was whether a crime could exist without will, and it had been established that it could not. You added that sin entered through one man. Yet the issue was not through what it began, but without what it could not exist.
translator_notes: The grammatical contrast is between “without will” and “through will”. The Latin prepositions govern different cases; Julian argues that Augustine has changed the question.

english: This detestable theft is plain. It was immediately punished by the retribution that clings to sins: before it could spread to destroy its hearers, it entrapped its own author. No one denies that the first human being incurred a sin. The question is how that sin could be found in newborn people. Define what you think the condition of the first sin was. You say, “There was free will, for sin cannot exist without will.” I approve this. But then you add, “Yet this sin, which cannot exist without will, clings to newborn people without will” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15).
Then your concession that sin does not exist without will is false, if, although committed through will, it could nevertheless pass to others without will.
Sin therefore now exists without will when it is found in those from whom you remove an evil will.
See, then, where your subtleties carry you. You try to persuade us that something does not exist through the very means by which it can exist.
That is, sin exists without will through the very fact that it cannot exist without will.

Thus it is to lose its own condition through its own condition, and exist without what it was defined as unable to exist without! This is denying reality. What comparable thing did Anaxagoras do when he said snow was black? You invent the claim that a thing’s nature is denied by its own fruits. Necessity and will are opposites, so that, as I showed above, they destroy one another by mutual conflict. Yet through a new and impossible alliance and a monstrous relationship, you make one arise as the other’s effect. You say necessity grew from the fruits of will, so that will erased itself by multiplying itself and changed its own condition through its activity. To state the matter in its own terms: after will began to be will, it ceased to be will. What could be imagined, I will not say more stupid, but more insane? Since these two, necessity and will, cannot coexist, and since you have confirmed my statement that an offense cannot exist without will, while also agreeing that infants have no will, you are dragged by the throat into admitting that there is no sin in them, since you professed that sin cannot exist without will.

As for your addition, “Through one man sin entered the world,” I have shown here how inappropriately it was placed, just as I explained in the second book how it should be understood. But now that the present argument is complete, I would like to reconsider your exceedingly sharp statement. You say: “‘Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12). Through that one man’s evil will, all sinned in him, when all were that one man. For that reason, each inherited original sin from him” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15). “They sinned then,” you say, “when all were that one man.”

I had already pointed out that you wrote this to Marcellinus (Augustine, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.11; 3.14). This testimony convicts you of believing and embracing the propagation of souls, taken particularly from Manichaeus’s very entrails; I quoted his statements in the third book. It is certainly so ugly that, although you imply it, you nevertheless never dare profess it. But let us postpone this for now: it is killed both by the obscenity of its first advocate and by the fear of his successor—that is, you. At present I want to examine the confusion that tosses you about in argument. You say, “Through that one man’s evil will, all sinned in him, when all were that one man.” If all were that one man, how did all sin through his evil will, when all these people whom you say were in him could have sinned by their own wills? Indeed, to turn the argument back, he was unhappier than everyone else, since he alone bears the odium, although according to your doctrine everyone sinned in him.

Infants therefore possessed will not only before they were born but before their great-grandparents were generated. They exercised choice before the seeds of their substance were created. Why, then, do you fear to say that at the time of their own conception they possess free will, by which they do not naturally inherit sin but voluntarily commit it, if you believe that those conceived today possessed sensation, judgment, and an effective will so many ages ago? You did not hesitate to state this in the books issued under Marcellinus’s name, plainly to show the madness that grips God’s enemies. There you say: “These infants sinned in Adam so that they might be created like him” (Augustine, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.11). What more false, insane, and filthy words could sound than that they sinned beforehand so that they might be created? That is, by acting they deserved to become beings who could act, and their action was older than their substance. It is enough to point out these inventions, more suited to Bacchic revels and ritual wands than to literature.

From this flowed your reply: “All sinned in him, when all were that one man, from whom each inherited original sin.” There is no need to labor here to show that, since will is a person’s act, will cannot exist before the person whose will it is. What I especially want understood is that even on this opinion there is no original sin. For if everyone who sinned was there, they inherited nothing from an original evil, because they all committed it through their own efforts. The inheritance of sin is therefore destroyed not only by catholic truth but by every argument of its own defender. That is indeed the nature of lies: they do not maintain a consistent pretense. Wasteful of shame and greedy for what belongs to another, they are exposed in everything they seize.
translator_notes: The supplied extraction included an Augustine paragraph beginning “Why does not Ambrose himself rather answer him?” after Julian’s speech. That reply, which addresses Julian directly, is excluded here. Romans 5:12 retains “in whom all sinned”, the wording at issue.

english: After this reply, he tries to wash away another point on which I had struck him. For after asking about infants’ will, I continued: “But you deny this”—that is, that a sinful will is present in newborn people—“and nevertheless say infants are under the devil. Nor do you conceal why you think they live under his power. You say, ‘Because they are born from the union of the two sexes, they are under the hostile power.’” The testimony of his own words therefore made it plain that he claims infants for the demon because they were born from the union of the two sexes. Through this I showed that he had enslaved marriage to the devil, although God instituted it and it cannot exist without union.

He now puts this before himself, beginning with my question: “So you say,” he writes, “that they are under the devil because they are born from the union of the two sexes?” Let us hear what explanation he gives. “I certainly say,” he replies, “that they are under the devil because of an offense. They are not free of the offense because they were born from that union which cannot perform even what is honorable without shameful lust. Ambrose, of most blessed memory, also said this” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15). What disastrous perversity in the man! What an unspeakable intention! What shameful falsehood!

Does this man dare to say he does not condemn marriage, to mock uneducated ears with such wickedness, and to claim that he has withdrawn from Manichaeus’s company? By repeated professions he places the union of the sexes, the act of marriage, and the parents’ feeling and sensation within the devil’s kingdom. Adding the help of his own sharpness to these Manichaean inventions, he pronounces the union devilish, located in both the act and the flesh of the married couple. Yet because of it he assigns the innocent to the devil’s kingdom, while acquitting those who perform the act! Always hostile to God in this way, he defends those who, according to him, serve the devil through lust.

But the infants whom he says God makes he assigns to the enemy’s dominion. Thus he accuses not the demon’s work, whose ministers he clears of guilt, but God’s work, which the pleasure conscious of the devil’s gift could not reach. So this accuser of marital activity, yet absolver of lusts, this assailant of innocence and slanderer of divine fairness, did not fear to write: “I certainly say that they are under the devil because they were born from that union.” Seeing the wickedness of this statement laid bare, he tried to defend it by some authority, which he could not produce from Scripture, and added that Bishop Ambrose had thought the same. It is no surprise that he accuses the dead when he also accuses the harmless.
translator_notes: The Latin web edition labels this speech Augustine, but the Italian parallel identifies Julian, and Augustine’s following reply confirms the attribution. The corrected speaker is retained.

english: How much more rightly you would say: “Manichaeus said the same thing in his letter to Patricius. He also said it in the letter he wrote to his daughter Menoch, and in many other writings that you have thoroughly absorbed.” Instead, you try to draw the bishop of Milan into your company. Because you cannot obtain a defense, you want to find consolation.
Do disputants’ writings count against God’s law or God’s work?

For the present, it is more than enough for me to prove even from this that you have nowhere read your belief in the sacred writings: in so important a case, you have produced nothing except the bishop’s little sayings, as you call them. If you had been able to find anything more authoritative, you would undoubtedly have left these alone.

But fortunately you first relieved me of the burden of such persons. In the book you composed to Timasius against free choice, holy Pelagius had recalled venerable men, both Ambrose and Cyprian, who had commended free choice in their books. You replied that their authority placed no burden upon you, even saying that if they had thought anything wrongly, they had atoned for it through progress toward a better life (compare Augustine, On Nature and Grace 71). Let your own words be returned to you so that you are ashamed to stir hostility from names alone. Yet the statements of Ambrose and the others whose reputation you strive to stain by associating them with your party can be defended by clear and kindly reasoning.

They may have spoken somewhat simply, or, while examining some other subject, may have had no need to meet questions arising on the side. They frequently praised marriage, thought no bodily feeling had been implanted by the devil, and did not subject God’s works—the members of nature—to the devil’s kingdom. They also explained, as occasions arose, marriage instituted by God and granted his blessing, and free choice. It is therefore humane to judge that they do not stand in fellowship with your wickedness if you find certain things ambiguously or carelessly placed in their writings. Just as the fact that all heresies conceal themselves behind some testimonies of holy Scripture and try to defend themselves by them does not count against Scripture, so I will not allow the reputation of catholic men to be surrendered because of some words poured out less cautiously. They did not intend to condemn marriage, deny free choice, or wound innocence. If they had intended this, they would not have strengthened your doctrine; they would have lost the honor of their office.

I therefore freely infer and pronounce that if any of them survived to the present day and saw the glory of Christian discipline extinguished, free will idle in everyone and trying to impute to necessity whatever it commits voluntarily, and disparagement of God’s works and overthrow of his law whispered into the people’s ears under the name of ineffective grace, he would be stirred against you with all his bitterness. Recognizing also that natural sin cannot be distinguished from Manichaean impiety, he would defend the catholic faith more plainly and more carefully, either correcting you or condemning you.

No one has the right to accept definitions and exclude their consequences. Therefore anyone who says infants belong to the devil’s jurisdiction because they are generated from sexual union undoubtedly condemns that union, in which nature acts, together with nature’s own institution.

Either both are denied together or both are accepted together. Although one can reject both, one cannot choose only one. It is, however, easier for an unlawful union to be burdened with the fault of will while the fruitfulness of its seeds remains defended, than for the sexual act to be vindicated while its fruits are accused. Your wavering between fear and impiety will therefore not establish new rules of argument, allowing you to accept one of two connected things and exclude what belongs to it. “Light-footed deer will graze in the sky” (1 Corinthians 15:20–23) (Virgil, Eclogues 1.59) before a conclusion can be denied after its premise has settled the matter.

The apostle Paul uses this form of argument when he says, “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. If Christ has not risen, your faith is empty” (1 Corinthians 15:16–17). But now Christ has risen; therefore it is certain that a day of resurrection awaits the dead (compare 1 Corinthians 15:20–23). To press this same point upon the reader with a shorter example: suppose there is doubt whether what is just is good. I ask whether you acknowledge that everything just is honorable. Once that is granted, I add another question: do you also pronounce everything honorable good? Once that too is granted, whether you like it or not, I conclude: if everything just is honorable, and everything honorable is good, then everything just is good. Anyone who tries to resist this conclusion after accepting the first premises does not shake reason’s structure but exposes himself to ridicule.

To bring the comparison back to the case: the question is whether sin exists in nature. I asked whether you would concede that no sin exists without will. You agreed, as your own words testify. I added whether you thought an infant possessed will. You denied this too. What follows as the third point, if sin does not exist without will? This is so certain that it cannot be doubted even by the Academics, whose wealth consists in holding nothing certain. So when you deny the third point after the first two premises, although it contains their conclusion, you do not overturn the foundations of reason: you reveal your frenzy.

added_allusions.reason: Christ has risen, ensuring the resurrection of others.

translator_notes: The source note gives 1 Corinthians 15:16, but the quotation includes verse 17.

english: Suppose, then, that the bishops whose words I am now clearing heard it doubted whether marital union was good. I would ask them whether they acknowledged that bodies were formed by God. Once that was granted, I would add whether they agreed that marriage was ordained by God. With that likewise confirmed, I would ask again whether offspring could exist without union. Once this was denied, what would follow? Clearly, if a body exists only through God, union only through a body, and offspring only through union, then both offspring and union belong to the same author as bodies.

Sensible men, catholic bishops, would undoubtedly agree to this conclusion. They would see that no one other than the true God had made anything in the flesh’s sensations or the offspring of the sexes; that God had made nothing evil; and that evil is nothing other than an evil will sinning without any compulsion from nature. They would surely pronounce that Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin had been shattered by the shining thunderbolts of catholic reasoning.

Stop accusing men of sound mind and leaders of churches. Let less careful remarks not be brought to judgment: a brief hesitation does not deserve anger, but a stubborn intention does. Let us instead imitate the zeal with which they built up their peoples by exhorting, beseeching, and rebuking. Would they have done any of this if, like you, they had believed sins natural rather than voluntary?

Let us proceed to the rest. Your claim that you assign offenses to the devil, not bodies, has absolutely no force. As I have frequently shown, you are simply denying the facts, with no aim except to avoid the odium of Manichaeus while breathing his poison. Bodies—quite plainly, bodies—are what you assign to the ruler of darkness: you profess their union devilish and accuse their reproductive organs, their movements, and their offspring. Following your earliest instruction, you openly accuse members, not vices. You call devilish the very thing that Manichaeus too resents seeing flourish in the sexes, as I showed from his writings.

To give the reader in brief repetition something he can retain: either show that infants possess will or remove the charge from them. When you fail to do this and instead assert that the devil possesses them because they were generated from bodily union, you show that you assign to the hostile power not sins, which do not exist without will, but bodies themselves. So the lust found in both human beings and animals is natural and instituted by God. But this lust you suffer in the inconsistency of your argument, through which you move among various and opposing doctrines, is conceived no less from stupidity than from impiety. I therefore rightly distinguish Ambrose from your company and do not call him a Manichaean, as you request.

You say Jovinian hurled this insult at him (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15), though I think you are lying here. But let us grant that you may at least be truthful in accusing Jovinian, and that he called Ambrose a Manichaean. That was plainly insane. He could not rightly be called a Manichaean when he preached that nature was good, sins voluntary, marriage instituted by God, and infants made by God. So if Jovinian thought that preferring virginity amounted to accusing marriage, he had no idea what he was saying. Opposition is one thing, ranking another. Praise of a good is a step toward better things; defamation of nature is a road to Manichaeus.

Since Ambrose did not condemn marriage or call marital union either the devil’s work or a necessity for sinning, Jovinian acted wickedly in comparing him with Manichaeus and thinking there was no difference between an accuser and a praiser of marriage. For if Ambrose said that those generated from lawful bodily union instituted by God had lied of their own will after they began to use reason, following the example of upright people, he nevertheless did not intend that union to seem a necessity for lying, but an indication of universality. His statement, “Those born from parents lie,” is like saying, “Every human being who governs his own choice has lied at some time.” (John 7:8–10) For he knew that no one except Christ had existed without the union of parents. Thus this sensible man meant marital activity to indicate not injustice but generality. He declared that Christ had avoided every lie, identifying him by the miracle of the woman who bore him. This thunders powerfully against Jerome, whose follower you are, who specifically tried to fasten a lie on Christ (compare John 7:8–10). Therefore someone who repeatedly praised creatures against your error was not rightly called a Manichaean, if he was called one at all.

added_allusions.reason: Repeats the accusation about Jerome’s treatment of Christ and the feast.

translator_notes: The supplied Latin reads “following the example of upright people”. This unusual wording is retained rather than silently changed to “wicked people”.

english: Yet although Jovinian is accused of hostility to Ambrose, he is acquitted when compared with you. When will the judgment of sensible people grant you enough credit to place you on the same level as Jovinian? He said there was a necessity for good; you, for evil. He said people were kept from error through the mysteries; you say they are not freed even through grace. He dissolved Mary’s virginity by the condition of childbirth; you transfer Mary herself to the devil by the condition of being born. He equates better things with good things—that is, virginity with marriage. You call marital union diseased and cheapen chastity by comparing it with something utterly foul. You do not insert a difference of degree between them; you change the whole category, preferring virginity not to a good but to an evil. It is the utmost cheapness to be pleasing only in comparison with something utterly disgusting.

Again, what did he do to insult God that resembles what you do? He wanted to weaken the force of God’s judgment on the side of kindness; you, on the side of malice. He says the good and the best will enjoy equal honor before God. You say the good and the impious—that is, the innocent and the devil—will be tormented by one punishment. He wants God to appear supremely merciful; you, supremely unjust. He says people initiated into God’s mysteries cannot sin. You contend that God himself sins: by weakness in the mysteries, by excess in his commands, and by cruelty in his judgments. Since the distance between you and Jovinian is as great as the closeness between you and Manichaeus, Jovinian is proved more tolerable than you to the same degree that Manichaeus is more dreadful than Jovinian.

But let us examine the rest. I think the reader has been instructed more than enough by what we have treated about the strength with which he either attacks anything in my statements or defends his own opinion. It will therefore not be necessary to demonstrate this by repeating all his writings. For he puts before himself scarcely more than isolated, scattered little lines from my book, often praising them and sometimes tickling them with the briefest criticism. Yet what he thinks he should bite at was not said by me in the way he supposes. I therefore direct the reader to my work: he will see that its argument agrees with truth.

This man, who complained that I accused him of attacking nature and seeds, could not endure continuous pretense. After soothing his patron’s hearing with tricks, he puts out his head like a tortoise. He had said that, unless Adam had sinned, people could have generated children as we ordinarily move our joints or trim our nails. Then he added: “But if the seed itself carries no curse, what does this passage in the book of Wisdom mean? ‘You were not ignorant that their race was wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning’” (Wisdom 12:10–11) (Psalm 58:4–5). He follows the testimony with this argument: “Surely, whoever these words concern, they concern human beings” (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.6.17–2.9.21).

Here is the man who professed to have abandoned Manichaean pursuits! Taking an opportunity from a statement he does not understand, he pronounces the seed cursed, malice natural, and the thought of the unjust incapable of change. It is said that those living beside the Nile’s cataracts have lost their hearing from the roar of the falling waters. Perhaps rumor invented that, spreading larger tales from great things. Still, the example serves to rebuke the deafness of fools who resist the voice of facts like deaf adders, amid the din of mutual intimidation (compare Psalm 58:4–5; LXX Psalm 57:5–6). Augustine cries: “The human race is wicked; its malice is natural; its thought forever unchangeable; its seed cursed from the beginning.” And there are still people who think he has not been stamped all over with Manichaeus’s mark! Let the public followers of that filth be questioned today. If they say anything different, let us be judged liars.

So if malice is natural, how do you pretend not to pronounce nature evil? If the seed is cursed from the beginning, how do you say you accuse the vices of wills, not of seeds? If evildoers’ thought cannot be changed, how do you falsely swear that you acknowledge free choice? Unless the only thing left is for you to say that those Hebrews, Sirach or Philo, who are uncertainly believed to have authored the book called Wisdom, were Manichaeans.

added_allusions.reason: Deaf adders refusing to hear.

english: The reader may now be waiting to learn how this testimony should be understood. The very man who appropriated it has shown that it concerns neither inherited sin nor the Manichaean opinion. For he says, “Whoever these words concern, they concern human beings.” (Wisdom 11:23–12:2) Surely, if it spoke of natural sin, it would speak not of some unspecified people but of everyone. The Manichaean opinion defames the nature of all mortals generally. But the statement under examination receives testimony even from its own plagiarist that it was pronounced not against everyone but against some. It is therefore clear that it had no business with inherited sin, since the statement strikes not at all but at a number of people.

Having shown that none of it concerns this profane opinion, let the writer’s soundness be defended by the testimony of his own book. He says to God: “You have mercy on everyone, because you can do everything, and you overlook human sins for the sake of repentance. For you love everything that exists, and you hate none of the things you have made. How could anything continue to exist unless you had willed it? You spare everything because it is yours, Lord, who love souls. For your good spirit is in all things. Therefore you correct those who stray little by little, and warn them about their sins, speaking to them so that they may abandon malice and believe in you, Lord” (Wisdom 11:23–12:2; Latin numbering 11:24–12:2).
translator_notes: The source’s Wisdom 11:24 begins at 11:23 in common modern numbering. Its “good spirit” differs from the familiar “immortal spirit” at Wisdom 12:1; the Latin wording is retained.

english: Do you see how hostile this grateful praise of God is to your opinion? It says that he creates souls and loves them. You deny this, swearing that innocent souls are under the devil and hated by God, though they possess nothing except what they received from their author.
Your doctrine also does not admit the repentance that the writer affirms God grants, since it contains the claim that evil is natural and wickedness cannot change.
His commendation of God’s warning sinners to abandon malice and believe in him entirely overturns the belief in natural evil. For it is certain that inborn things cannot be abandoned.

Having explained God’s patience and his most gentle ordering of things, by which he does not desire the death of the dying person but rather that he turn back and live (compare Ezekiel 18:32; 33:11), the writer continues to prove what he said by examples. He mentions those whose terribly wicked lives in the land of Canaan had kindled the Almighty’s anger, so that the land would be granted, through the most just punishment, to the victories of the Israelites, now living under God’s law. “Hating those ancient inhabitants of your holy land, because they did hateful deeds before you through spells and unjust sacrifices, and were merciless killers of children, you willed to destroy them through our fathers’ hands, so that the land dearest to you of all lands might receive a worthy settlement of God’s children” (Wisdom 12:3–7) (Ezekiel 18:32).

He testifies why God wished the seven nations to perish, after whose destruction for the most part the promised land was given to the Israelites (compare Deuteronomy 7:1–2). Lest God appear to distinguish persons by partiality within one human nature, he explains why the Canaanites deserved to be killed. “You hated,” he says, “those ancient inhabitants of your holy land.” (Ezekiel 33:11) Why? According to you, he should certainly have added: because they were generated from a devilish union; because the ruler of darkness possessed them; because Adam infected everyone who would come from his stock. But he says none of these things. What reason does he give for the hatred? Only deeds committed through free will. “You hated them,” he says, “because they did deeds hateful to you.” (Deuteronomy 7:1–2)

But so that we would not be ignorant of the deeds, and so that you could not call these acts of the nations reproductive desire, he details the kinds of action themselves. “Through spells,” he says, “and unjust sacrifices; and they were merciless killers of children.” That is, they served sorcery and sacrifices that were unjust because they were offered to idols, after worship of the Creator had been abandoned. To these sacrileges they devoted their own relatives, appeasing demons even by the enormity of murdering their children. See, then, how far he is from speaking of the crime Manichaeus invents, a crime naturally adhering to every mortal. He recalls that their chief offense was that they did not refrain even from destroying their own little children. Those children’s deaths would not bring odium on the killer if both the murderer and the child displeased God because of one and the same sin.

added_allusions.reason: God desires the dying person’s turning and life, not death.
God desires the wicked person’s turning and life, not death.
Seven nations displaced when Israel receives the promised land.

english: “Yet even these,” he says, “you spared as human beings, and sent wasps ahead of the army—not because you lacked the power to subject the impious to the righteous in battle, but, judging little by little, you gave them room for repentance” (Wisdom 12:8–10) (Genesis 9:20–27). “You pricked even those sacrilegious people,” he says in effect, “with the stings of flies, so that from the trivial instrument of their affliction they might recognize the avenger’s power.” After God’s purpose and the form of punishment made clear the voluntary sins whose rejection was awaited and sought, only then does the writer’s rebuke rise against the stubborn impiety of those punished. He says they had entered into such familiarity with crimes that these seemed in a way inborn. “You were not ignorant,” he says, “that their race had been most wicked, that their malice was natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for they were a cursed seed from the beginning. Nor did you grant pardon for their sins out of fear of anyone” (Wisdom 12:10–11).

He means: “Although you so kindly and patiently granted time for repentance and set up a watchtower of warning, to defend your justice and mercy against every slander and every suspicion of cruelty, they nevertheless despised your warnings after despising your earlier benefits.” They acted as though wishing to prove that they came from the seed of Ham, against whom blessed Noah, after his nakedness was mocked, had hurled curses in fatherly judgment (compare Genesis 9:20–27). Why be surprised, then, that the writer recalled the severe sentence that had struck their ancestor for his insolence, to disgrace descendants who did not cease imitating him? In the Law, imitation by descendants is frequently rebuked using terms of kinship. Thus the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). Daniel is also read rebuking the filthy elders, though they came from Israel’s stock, in the same way: “Seed of Canaan, not of Judah” (Daniel 13:56; Susanna 56). The prophet Ezekiel likewise reproaches the people of Jerusalem: “Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite” (Ezekiel 16:3, 45).

This is therefore an established usage: defamation of ancestry is added to blame of the will. A person appears to cling excessively to crime when, because of that crime, even his seed suffers insult. The same custom is also observed on the side of good people: when a man appears upright in every way, he is said to flourish with inborn virtues. Thus blessed Job affirms that he drew from the breasts the compassionate feeling with which he helped the needy, or rather that it came with him from his mother’s womb (Job 31:18). No comparison, exaggeration, or ambiguity can therefore count against plain facts. It is certain that mortals are never required to correct natural properties, yet God commands human beings to desist from evil. It is thus proved with the utmost truth that natural sin cannot exist.

added_allusions.reason: Noah’s nakedness, Ham, and the ancestral curse.

translator_notes: Julian names Ham as the recipient of Noah’s curse; Genesis 9:25 names Canaan. His statement is retained with the biblical passage linked. Daniel 13:56 belongs to Susanna in Bibles that print this account separately. Job 31:18 is paraphrased in the wording Julian uses, without substitution from a modern Bible.

english: Wisdom continues: “Who will accuse you if nations you made perish, when there is no other God besides you, who cares for all? But since you are just, you order all things justly. You consider condemning someone who should not be punished foreign to your power, for your power is the beginning of justice” (Wisdom 12:12–16). This certainly agrees with the common reasoning of sensible people that justice is the greatest mark of God—a justice that Manichaeus and the advocate of inherited sin deny with every effort of their fables.

A little later it continues: “By chastising them you made your children full of good hope, because when you judge you give room for repentance amid sins. For if you delivered the enemies of your servants, who deserved death, with so much affliction by way of warning, giving time and opportunity through which malice could be changed, with what care do you judge your children, to whose fathers you gave oaths and covenants containing good promises? Therefore, when you discipline us, you scourge our enemies many times over, so that we may reflect on your goodness in judging” (Wisdom 12:19–22).
translator_notes: The source note spans Wisdom 12:16–22; the quoted words begin at 12:19. The Latin’s language of delivering the enemies through afflictive warning is retained rather than replaced with familiar modern wording.

english: You see, then, what a distinction the surface of the words makes between the natures of the two peoples: it calls the Israelites God’s children and the Canaanites a cursed seed. If the sound of these words referred to generation and birth, one would have to say that the generation of the devout differed from that of the profane.

Yet even according to this nonsense, it would still be clear that the first sin was not inherited, since the seeds of so many nations together would plainly show that its transmission had been interrupted.

But just as the praise spoken of the Jews does not mean that anyone should be believed to shine with inborn holiness, so calling malice natural does not mean that the seeds are being declared defective. The constitution of nature is unshakable, and whatever it possesses it receives from God its author. Without counting against that nature, this variety of words marks either the force of rebuke or the work of praise.

Just as the seed is called cursed here, elsewhere, in a reading of greater authority, it is called blessed. For the prophet Isaiah says of the Israelites: “They will build houses and inhabit them themselves; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit themselves. They will not build for others to inhabit, or plant for others to eat. For the days of my people will be like the days of the tree of life. The works of their lips endure. My chosen ones will not labor in vain or beget children under a curse, because they are seed blessed by God” (Isaiah 65:21–23).
translator_notes: This quotation follows a different textual form from many modern Bibles, including “tree of life”, “works of their lips”, and children born “under a curse”. These readings are translated as given.

english: Let little children wrestle with a question arising from these contradictions of words, and, capable of nothing greater than sounds, fight over the cups that amuse them. The catholic faith does not believe God’s law quarrels with itself, nor does it admit any authority that destroys reason. It listens to no opinion or flattery that stains divine fairness. Rather, it not only believes but knows God to be creator of all natures; it imputes sin to nothing other than free will. Through all these things it has no doubt that the inheritance of sin is false.
